name: Meritocratic systems
purpose: What is the promise of meritocracy – and why is it questioned in selection?

parts.label: Premise
points: Actors are rewarded for talent and hard work
Framed as the way to a fair society and productive organizations

parts.label: In a meritocracy
points: Riches and rule are earned, not inherited (vs aristocracy)
Power and privilege allocated by individual merit, not social background

parts.label: IQ + Effort = Merit
points: But what looks like merit on a CV is partly produced by class origins

apply: Ask how each candidate's “merit” was produced (opportunities, capitals, networks)
Separate the signal on the CV from the job-relevant capability
pitfalls: Treating prestige signals (top school, unpaid internships) as pure merit
example: Chris Sands (EIC) chooses between John and Peter, childhood friends who both fit EIC's culture – part B reveals their very different back stories.

name: Bourdieu's three capitals
origin: Bourdieu · as used by Ingram (2021): “social class origins”
purpose: Which resources produce social inequality – and shape a candidate's CV?

parts.label: Economic capital
points: Command over financial resources: cash, assets
→ can afford unpaid internships, travel, tuition

parts.label: Social capital
points: Resources from group membership, relations, networks of influence and support
→ referrals, insider tips

parts.label: Cultural capital
points: Knowledge, skills, education, high expectations
Any advantage giving higher standing
→ “polish”, confident interviewing, cultural fit

apply: Map each candidate's advantages to the three capitals
Ask which skills the less-advantaged candidate built instead (resilience, work experience, responsibility)
Recommend selection methods that measure capability rather than capitals
pitfalls: Mixing the capitals up: networks = social, education/manners = cultural, money = economic
example: Peter's work experience may reveal capabilities that a prestige-oriented CV screen undervalues.

name: Signaling theory in selection
purpose: Why do recruiters rely on degrees and similar signals – and when does that mislead them?

parts.label: Expensive to obtain
points: Only able/committed candidates invest

parts.label: Granted by screening institutions
points: Universities, programmes pre-select the pool

parts.label: Require acquiring knowledge
points: The signal implies skills

parts.label: But: signals can be biased
points: Cost of the signal depends on capitals, not only ability
How much evidentiary weight should a signal get once we know how it was produced?
“Evidence-based” selection ≠ reading the evidence literally

apply: Name the signals in the CVs
Explain how they were produced and who could afford them
HR challenge: distinguish the signal from the underlying job-relevant capability – use work samples, structured interviews
pitfalls: Rejecting signals altogether – they carry information, but need to be weighted

name: Person–organisation fit vs “cultural fit”
purpose: Can the search for fit reproduce inequality?

parts.label: P–O fit
points: Match between person's values/goals and the organisation's
Legitimate selection criterion (Inditex)

parts.label: The problem
points: How cultural fit is defined and assessed
Fit judged as “like us” → similar-to-me bias
Reproduces homogeneity and inequality

apply: Define fit by job-relevant values and behaviours, write it down in advance, assess it with several raters
pitfalls: Using “fit” as an unexplained gut feeling

name: Inequality, discrimination, bias
purpose: Three related but NOT interchangeable concepts.

parts.label: Inequality
points: Unequal outcomes between groups

parts.label: Discrimination
points: Differential treatment associated with group membership

parts.label: Bias
points: A cognitive/attitudinal process

apply: Name precisely what the case shows: an outcome gap (inequality), unequal treatment (discrimination) or a judgement error (bias)
An outcome gap alone does not prove discrimination – candidates may differ (→ field experiments)
pitfalls: Using the three words as synonyms

name: Common biases in people perception
purpose: Which subjective biases distort recruitment and selection decisions?

parts.label: Halo effect
points: One positive feature → see only positives

parts.label: Horns effect
points: Same, but only negatives

parts.label: Similar-to-me
points: Oneself as the “gold standard”

parts.label: Stereotyping
points: Prejudiced assumptions from appearance or background: ethnicity, gender, age, dialect/accent

parts.label: Self-delusion
points: Believing oneself immune from bias

apply: Spot the bias in the case decision and name it
Match a remedy: structured interviews and scoring (halo/horns), diverse panels (similar-to-me), anonymised CVs (stereotyping), training + monitoring data (self-delusion)
pitfalls: Naming a bias without showing where it appears in the case
example: The surgeon riddle (“I cannot operate on this boy, he is my son”): the doctor is his mother – unconscious gender stereotypes.

name: Unconscious bias in R&S practices
origin: Gaucher et al. (2011) · Bell (2013) · Austin & Pisano (2017)
purpose: How does unconscious bias enter the design of recruitment and selection?

parts.label: Gendered wording
points: Masculine wording in job ads maintains inequality in male-dominated occupations (Gaucher et al., 2011)

parts.label: In-group favouritism
points: Hiring, promoting, rewarding the “in” group constrains diversity, against women and minorities (Bell, 2013)

parts.label: Conformity to standard methods
points: Absolute conformity to standardized approaches screens out neurodiverse people (Austin & Pisano, 2017)

apply: Audit the case's job ad, referral practices and assessment format for these three mechanisms
pitfalls: Standardization is good for reliability – but must allow reasonable adjustments

name: Measuring discrimination: field experiments
purpose: If one group is hired less often, how do we know it is discrimination and not differences between candidates?

parts.label: Equivalent applicants
points: Researchers construct applications equal in job-relevant characteristics

parts.label: Vary the cue
points: Only racial/ethnic cues differ (e.g. names)

parts.label: Compare callbacks
points: Discrimination ratio = callback rate of white natives / callback rate of target group

parts.label: Causal inference
points: The gap can only come from the cue → discrimination
Real applicants differ in many ways – comparing them cannot show this

apply: Explain why a firm's raw hiring statistics are not proof – and how a correspondence test would settle it
example: Meta-analysis of 97 field experiments, 200,000+ applications, nine countries in Europe and North America; France shows the highest discrimination relative to the US (≈ 1.43), Germany the lowest (≈ 0.92).

name: Why reduce bias and increase diversity?
purpose: What is the business case for diversity – beyond fairness?

parts.label: More innovative
points: Firms with more heterogeneous ethnic and disciplinary backgrounds innovate more

parts.label: Substitutes?
points: Disciplinary diversity can be substituted by intense external collaboration
Ethnic diversity can neither be replaced nor complemented by external sources

parts.label: Type of innovation
points: Disciplinary diversity → radical and incremental
Ethnic diversity → mainly radical

apply: Use as the performance argument for inclusive selection, next to the fairness argument

name: R&S core ideas: an inclusive process
purpose: How can EIC (and other organizations) improve candidate selection and make it more inclusive?

parts.label: Carefully design the process
points: Systematic & transparent criteria (set in advance)
Validity, reliability & practicability
Put standard signals and preconceptions into question

parts.label: Involve a variety of actors
points: Reduce unconscious bias
Increase diversity

parts.label: What employers do (CIPD)
points: Diverse interview panels
Training interviewers on legal obligations and objective practice
Criteria determined in advance and linked to the job
Removing biographical details from initial screening
Monitoring data on protected characteristics
EDI statements, flexible-working ads, checking ad wording

apply: Turn the three blocks into concrete recommendations for the case firm, each linked to the bias it reduces
pitfalls: Generic “more diversity” recommendations without a mechanism
